conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum/Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days, and it helps us spot anything that might benefit from extra support. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell us you’re in immediate danger; then we work together on safety. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to start?

1. Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly? It’s been hard. I used to laugh all the time—little jokes, silly memes, whatever—but now it feels like I’m too tired or just… flat. Sometimes my partner tries to lighten the mood and I can tell it’s supposed to be funny, but I can’t really laugh; I just give a half-smile and look back at the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really. Most of the time I feel like I’m stuck behind this fog—like I can see that something’s supposed to be funny, but it just doesn’t reach me. I might force a little chuckle so people don’t worry, but genuine laughter hasn’t happened much at all this week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. When I think about anything coming up—coffee with a friend, even just a walk—I don’t feel that little spark I used to. I still go, because I know I should, but it’s more like I’m dragging myself. Mostly I catch myself thinking, “What’s the point?” and then feeling guilty for being so negative.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If she’s fussy and won’t nap, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I missed her sleepy window or I’m not soothing her the “right” way. When the pacifier falls on the floor, I’ll replay how I should’ve been holding it tighter. I know in my head it’s not rational, but the guilt just pops up and sits there.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay, or I’ll check the monitor ten times because I’m sure I heard something. There’s usually no real reason—she’s healthy, the doctor says she’s doing great—but I can’t shake the “what if” thoughts. They buzz around like mosquitoes until I’m exhausted from swatting them away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week, yeah. It’s like my heart suddenly starts racing and I get this tight feeling in my chest—like something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s going on. I’ll be rocking her in the nursery and out of nowhere I’m convinced I’m not doing enough, or that something’s wrong with her even though she’s sleeping peacefully. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Most of the time it feels like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finish one feeding and think, “Okay, maybe I can nap,” but then she stirs or there’s laundry or bottles to wash, and it just piles up. I keep telling myself I should be able to handle it—other moms seem to—but the list never ends and I end up staring at the wall feeling like I’m drowning in small stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening almost every night. I’ll finally get her down in the bassinet, crawl into bed myself, and then my brain just switches on—playing back everything I think I did wrong, worrying about the next feed, feeling guilty for feeling so low. I’ll lie there for an hour or two, drift off for a bit, and then wake up again. Even when the baby’s sleeping a longer stretch, I can’t seem to stay asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll look at her little face and feel so much love, but then this heaviness creeps in and I just feel… empty. Sometimes I’ll cry while I’m folding her onesies, not even sure why—it just feels like I’m stuck in a rut I can’t climb out of.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes... it’s happened a few times. Yesterday I burst into tears while I was trying to sterilize the bottles—just overwhelmed by nothing in particular. And the night before, my partner asked how my day was and I couldn’t even get the words out; I just sat on the couch and cried. It feels like the tears are right under the surface all the time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I just want to feel like myself again so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared that since your baby arrived you feel enveloped by a persistent gray fog: joy and laughter feel out of reach, daily tasks seem insurmountable, and waves of guilt, worry, and tearfulness arrive without warning. Despite your deep love for your daughter, you describe an <sym>emptiness</sym>, <sym>insomnia</sym>, and frequent <sym>crying spells</sym> that leave you exhausted and convinced you're falling short.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>"Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself 'a lot' and gives multiple examples of persistent, intrusive self-blame over minor infant-care mishaps, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive, persistent anxiety on most days with compulsive checking behaviors, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes multiple discrete episodes of sudden intense anxiety with physical symptoms (racing heart, chest tightness) and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes" in frequency and severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant overwhelm, inability to manage daily tasks, and feeling like drowning, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep directly linked to unhappiness and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Pretty much every day" aligns with "Yes, most of the time" and captures pervasive sadness.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple recent crying episodes triggered by ordinary situations, indicating frequent but not constant tearfulness.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse key <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, fatigue, diminished ability to think or concentrate, and recurrent thoughts of inadequacy. <quote>I just feel… empty</quote> and <quote>like I'm drowning in small stuff</quote> mirror severe functional impairment. No self-harm ideation is present, so acute safety risk is lower, yet symptom intensity warrants prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health team</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or sertraline-compatible <med>antidepressant medication</med> suitable for breastfeeding
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress
4. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula-to cover night feeds and household tasks so you can obtain 4-6 hour stretches of sleep
5. Practice 5-minute grounding or breathing exercises when <sym>panic symptoms</sym> surface; consider a mindfulness app designed for new mothers
6. Contact local or online support groups (e.g., Postpartum Support International warmline 1-800-944-4773) for peer encouragement
7. Keep a simple mood log and sleep hours to share with your clinician at your next visit
8. If any thoughts of self-harm emerge, seek emergency care or call 988 (U.S.) or your local crisis line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [insert today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS dialogue):

1. Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, emptiness  
2. Marked anhedonia; activities performed out of obligation only  
3. Pervasive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
4. Unprompted anxious “what-if” ruminations and monitor-checking  
5. Discrete panic-like episodes (racing heart, dread) several times/week  
6. Overwhelmed, “drowning” in routine tasks; compares self unfavorably to others  
7. Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to intrusive worry/guilt  
8. Daily sadness and feeling “stuck” despite expressed love for baby  
9. Frequent crying spells (e.g., during bottle prep, when asked about day)  
10. Denies any self-harm or suicidal ideation  

Pattern: High endorsement of depressive and anxiety symptoms; no safety concerns voiced.

Screening significance  
- Elevated risk for major postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety  
- Functional impairment (sleep, coping, self-care) apparent  
- No self-harm ideation → current low acute risk, but continued monitoring warranted  

Next steps: Discuss results with patient; offer formal assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7) and referral to OB mental-health team or perinatal psychiatry.
